page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question
Classification of Elements – Periodic Properties · 2 marks

steps.label: The law
lines: Dobereiner's law of triads: when elements
with similar properties are arranged in
groups of three in the increasing order of
their atomic weights, the atomic weight of
the middle element is nearly the arithmetic
steps.why: The law is a numerical pattern, so its statement must contain the numbers' rule: three similar elements, increasing atomic weight, middle equals the mean of the outer two.
common_mistakes: Writing atomic numbers. Dobereiner worked long before atomic numbers; the law uses atomic weights.
Leaving out that the three elements have similar properties. Any three elements do not form a triad.
steps.memory_tip: A triad is three similar elements where the middle one averages the outer two by weight.
steps.margin_note: Three parts: similar elements, groups of three, middle equals the mean.

steps.label: The example
lines: The properties of sodium are intermediate
between those of lithium and potassium.
steps.why: The alkali metal triad is the standard example because the mean works out exactly: the average of 7 and 39 is 23, sodium's atomic weight.
common_mistakes: Quoting the triad without the arithmetic. The calculation (7 + 39)/2 = 23 is the evidence.
Mixing elements from different families into one triad.
steps.memory_tip: 7, 23, 39 — each step is 16, so the middle is the exact average.
steps.margin_note: Ca, Sr, Ba and Cl, Br, I are equally accepted triads.

insider_note: The example is a full mark and it is arithmetic rather than names — the working line is what gets ticked. Li, Na, K is the safest triad because the mean comes out exactly.
